sections.html:
The Recorder's office is at 1415 Melody Lane, Building B, in Bisbee, Arizona 85603. Walk-in service runs weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm. Bisbee staff also maintain the county's voter rolls, though a home seller only touches the property-records side.

Contact methodNumber or address
Street address1415 Melody Lane, Building B, Bisbee, AZ 85603
HoursMonday to Friday, 8 am to 5 pm
Phone520-432-8350
Toll free888-457-4513
Fax520-432-8368

Distances here are long, so a quick call can save a drive. In most sales you will not go at all, since escrow submits the deed on your behalf.

The county charges one flat price of $30 for recording a document, set by A.R.S. 11-475. Government agencies pay $15. Military discharge papers are free to record under A.R.S. 11-465. Other charges at the counter:

  • Copies: $1 per page.
  • Certifying a copy: $3 per document.
  • Mail or email processing: $1.
  • Subdivision plat or survey map: $24 for the first sheet.

The fee schedule has no extra county transfer tax line. Should an unfamiliar recording charge show up in your closing paperwork, ask escrow to explain it before you sign.

No sale deed gets recorded here without either a finished affidavit or an exemption number, and staff will turn it away if both are missing. For help with the form itself, call the Arizona Department of Revenue at 602-716-6843.

The affidavit is the state's record of what really changed hands. Under A.R.S. 11-1133 both sides sign it. Expect to supply each party's name and mailing address, where future tax statements should go, the legal description, the sale date, total consideration, how the purchase is financed, the parcel number, and whether the buyer will live in the home or rent it.

Section 11-1134 sets out the exemptions. If you claim one, write it on the deed. Common examples include gifts, court-ordered transfers, tax-delinquency sales, and token-price transfers inside a family, such as between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, or siblings.

sections.h2: What happens after the deed reaches the Recorder?
sections.html:
A complete document that follows the layout rules and comes with the right payment is accepted and becomes a permanent public record. After that:

  1. Data entry staff key the main details into an index.
  2. The microfilm department films and scans the document.
  3. The original is mailed to the return address you typed on it.
  4. If the original is later lost, you can order a certified copy.

Mailed originals take 15 to 20 business days to return. On an ordinary sale, escrow handles all of this, so ask your officer for the recording date instead of waiting on the mailbox.

sections.h2: Where recording fits in a closing
sections.html:
For a typical sale the order is simple. The buyer and seller sign at escrow, the title company pays off any existing loan and the current tax balance from your proceeds, and then it submits the deed and the affidavit to the Recorder. Your sale is complete for practical purposes once the deed is recorded, so ask for a copy of the recorded deed or the recording date for your files.

If anything in the package is wrong, the Recorder rejects it and the closing can slip. That is why a seller who has checked names, the legal description and signatures against the title commitment is in a better position than one who waits for the title company to catch it.

sections.h2: Getting copies of a deed or plat
sections.html:
Deed copies can be requested at the counter or by mail. Each page costs $1, or $2 if the office faxes it. A copy of a survey or plat map is $5.00 a page when you can give the book and page of the map.

Certifying any copy adds $3 per document. Copies of maps run $3 at 11 by 17 inches and $1 at 8 1/2 by 11 inches. If you are the one recording a map, the first sheet is $24 and each additional sheet is $20, with lower rates for government agencies.

sections.h2: What the Recorder can and cannot tell you
sections.html:
The index is built on grantor and grantee names. You can search it yourself at the counter, or have a title company do the digging. Looking up an owner by parcel number is not something this office does; that call goes to the Assessor at 520-432-8650.

  • Liens: search the name index yourself or ask a title company.
  • A past selling price: find the affidavit that was recorded with that sale.
  • Foreclosure history: bring the owner's name or a street address.
  • Name changes on a deed, trusts and removing someone who has died: see a title company or attorney.

Blank recording forms come from stationery or office supply stores. For homestead questions the office refers people to A.R.S. 33-1101 and an attorney, and for business names to A.R.S. 44-1236. Staff can explain what they record, but they cannot advise you on how to hold title.

Recording closes out a sale, but a few special papers may need to land here first. A beneficiary deed only works if it was recorded before the owner died (A.R.S. 33-405). An affidavit of succession for a small estate is recorded here once the court registrar issues a certified copy (A.R.S. 14-3971). After a tax lien sale, a certificate of redemption may be recorded here too (A.R.S. 42-18154).

If your house involves any of these, round up whatever has already been recorded and give it to the title company, which can list what must be cleared before the buyer's deed goes on record. A sale with no lender involved removes one party who would otherwise need the title cleaned up.

sections.h2: What to have ready before recording
sections.html:
A rejected package means a second round of mail, so run through this list with your escrow officer first:

  1. The deed carries the caption, original signatures and the notary acknowledgment.
  2. The legal description and parcel number match your tax bill.
  3. A completed affidavit or an exemption note is attached.
  4. The return address typed on the document is one where you can actually receive mail.
  5. The $30 fee, or the correct amount for extra documents, is included.

On an inherited home, also ask whether an earlier deed, an affidavit of succession or the release of an old loan is still unrecorded. Those go in ahead of the buyer's deed so the title trail has no gaps.

Cochise County spans 6,219 square miles of Arizona's southeastern corner on the Mexican border, with 125,447 residents in 2020. Bisbee holds the county seat, and Sierra Vista is the biggest city. Owners who live far away can usually finish the recording steps by phone, by mail or through a title company.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Cochise County?
faqs.a: Record it at the Cochise County Recorder, 1415 Melody Lane, Building B, Bisbee, AZ 85603. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8 am to 5 pm, and the phone is 520-432-8350.

faqs.q: How much does the Cochise County Recorder charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The fee is a flat $30 per document, or $15 for government agencies, under A.R.S. 11-475. Copies are $1 a page and certification is $3.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get my recorded documents back?
faqs.a: Allow 15 to 20 business days. The original returns to the address typed on the document.

faqs.q: Do I need an affidavit of real property value to record a sale deed?
faqs.a: Yes, unless an exemption applies. The Recorder requires a completed affidavit or an exemption number on every sale, and the Arizona Department of Revenue can answer form questions.

faqs.q: Can the Recorder tell me who owns a parcel?
faqs.a: No. Owner-by-parcel questions go to the Assessor at 520-432-8650. The Recorder searches by grantor and grantee name.
